    Cystic lung disease — quick reference

    This exercise scores a case's major pattern (the dominant, most extensive finding) and, when present, a minor pattern (a second, less extensive finding) separately — each with its own axial (central/peripheral/diffuse), subpleural-sparing, and vertical (upper/lower/diffuse) distribution.

    Emphysema — centrilobular or paraseptal lucencies without a true perceptible wall; classically upper-zone predominant in centrilobular (smoking-related) disease.

    Honeycombing — clustered, thick-walled cystic airspaces in rows, subpleural and basal-predominant, no zonal sparing. The imaging hallmark of end-stage fibrosis (UIP).

    Bronchiectasis — dilated, thick-walled airways (signet-ring sign, tram tracks); central or peripheral depending on cause (e.g., ABPA is central, post-infectious/traction bronchiectasis from fibrosis is peripheral).

    Miscellaneous (thick-walled cystic lesion, LCH, LAM, LIP, aging lung, etc.) — true cysts with a thin, definable wall. LCH: bizarre/irregular upper-mid zone cysts with subpleural sparing, often with nodules, in young smokers. LAM: innumerable thin-walled round cysts diffusely throughout the lung with no zonal or subpleural sparing, associated with angiomyolipoma/tuberous sclerosis. LIP: scattered perivascular cysts, often with Sjögren's or other CTD.

    Other (reticulation, GGO, nodules, etc.) — a catch-all for a non-cystic/non-emphysematous secondary pattern superimposed on or accompanying the major finding.

    Anatomical distortion (traction bronchiectasis, architectural distortion) — marks irreversible fibrotic disease rather than a purely airspace or airway process.

    General teaching framework — provided as a reference for interpreting the categories tested here, not a case-specific diagnosis. The minor-pattern sub-fields are only assessed when minor findings are present.
